faq.a: Cytogenetics stratifies risk; favorable lesions (t(8;21), inv(16)) have higher remission rates, while adverse lesions (complex karyotype, FLT3‑ITD) may need alternative agents or transplant.
faq.q: Why is cytogenetics important if treatment is the same for all patients?

faq.a: Yes; many patients have normal or low WBC with marrow packed with blasts; always examine the smear.
faq.q: Can AML present without a high white‑cell count?

faq.a: If available, it rapidly reduces leukocyte load in hyperleukocytosis; otherwise, start hydroxyurea to lower counts while arranging transfer.
faq.q: What is the role of leukapheresis in low‑resource hospitals?

exam: A 30‑year‑old HIV‑positive man presents with fatigue, bruising, and 30 % blasts on smear – what is your next diagnostic step? — Obtain bone‑marrow aspirate for morphology, flow, and cytogenetics.
You see Auer rods on a peripheral smear – how does this influence your differential? — Confirms myeloid lineage, favors AML over ALL.
WBC is 150 × 10⁹/L with dyspnea – what emergency measure should you consider? — Initiate leukapheresis or hydroxyurea to prevent leukostasis.
Patient develops fever and neutrophils 0.3 × 10⁹/L after induction – what is the immediate management? — Start broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics, obtain cultures, and consider antifungal prophylaxis.
Cytogenetics shows FLT3‑ITD – how does this affect prognosis and therapy? — Indicates adverse risk; consider adding FLT3 inhibitor if available, plan for early transplant.
A child with 15 % blasts is suspected of AML – why is this still AML? — WHO criteria require ≥20 % blasts, but certain recurrent genetic lesions (e.g., t(8;21)) define AML regardless of percentage.
Why is high‑dose cytarabine avoided in a patient with renal failure? — It accumulates, causing neuro‑toxicity; choose alternative consolidation.
What supportive measure reduces early mortality in AML? — Prompt transfusion of platelets when <10 × 10⁹/L and red cells for symptomatic anemia.
ai.title: Acute Myeloid Leukemia
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is a clonal proliferation of myeloid blasts that replaces normal marrow, causing cytopenias and rapid clinical decline. Diagnosis relies on morphology, immunophenotype, and genetics; treatment is urgent chemotherapy and supportive care.

b: Incidence rises after age 40; median age in Africa ~35‑40 due to earlier exposure to infections and toxins.
sections.p: AML is a heterogeneous malignancy of the myeloid line, presenting with anemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, and often organ infiltration. It is the commonest adult acute leukemia in sub‑Saharan Africa.

b: Immunophenotype: CD13, CD33, CD117, MPO positivity; CD34 variable.
sections.p: Diagnosis requires ≥20 % myeloid blasts in marrow or blood, plus exclusion of other causes. Cytogenetics (e.g., t(8;21), inv(16), FLT3‑ITD) guide risk stratification.

t.b: Does the patient have circulating blasts? Presence confirms suspicion; absence does not rule out AML.
Quantifies blast percentage and allows morphology; essential for diagnosis.
Identifies myeloid immunophenotype; distinguishes AML from ALL.
Risk stratifies; informs choice of intensive vs. low‑intensity therapy. If unavailable, use clinical risk (age, WBC count).
Shows cytopenias and blast count; guides urgency of treatment.
Detects tumor lysis risk; elevated LDH supports high turnover.

b: Leukostasis risk when WBC >100 × 10⁹/L – consider emergent leukapheresis if available.
Tumor lysis syndrome risk after chemotherapy – hydrate, monitor electrolytes.
sections.p: Patients present with fatigue, infections, bleeding, and sometimes organomegaly or leukostasis. Early recognition prevents fatal complications such as intracranial hemorrhage or septic shock.

b: Always ask about recent infections (HIV, TB) and exposure to benzene or pesticides.
When blasts are seen, the next step is bone‑marrow confirmation, not immediate chemotherapy.
sections.p: Examiners test integration of presentation, investigations, and urgent management steps.

b: Induction: cytarabine + anthracycline (e.g., daunorubicin). Chosen for proven remission rates; avoid idarubicin if cardiac disease.
Avoid high‑dose cytarabine in severe renal impairment – risk of neuro‑toxicity.
Transfusion support for symptomatic anemia or platelets <10 × 10⁹/L.
Broad‑spectrum antibiotics for neutropenic fever; antifungal prophylaxis if prolonged neutropenia.
sections.p: Treatment is two‑phased: induction chemotherapy to achieve remission, then consolidation (high‑dose cytarabine or stem‑cell transplant when feasible). Supportive care is vital.

t.b: Identify pathogen in febrile neutropenia; guides targeted antibiotics.
Dose‑adjust chemotherapy; avoid nephrotoxic agents if creatinine >2 mg/dL.
Detect DIC; replace platelets or plasma as needed.

b: ALL: lymphoid markers (CD19, TdT) and often younger age.
sections.p: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) can mimic AML early.

b: A low WBC count does not rule out AML – blasts can be low in marrow‑only disease.
Fever may be absent despite severe neutropenia.
sections.p: Peripheral smear may miss blasts if sampling is poor; normal LDH does not exclude aggressive disease.

b: Starting empiric antibiotics without confirming neutropenia severity.
Delaying bone‑marrow biopsy because of limited pathology services – arrange referral early.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe bleeding, neurological deficits, or respiratory distress – possible leukostasis or DIC.
Fever >38 °C with neutrophils <0.5 × 10⁹/L – urgent infection control.
